text:
So, with keys, one row can point at another. And it turns out those links only come in a few shapes. One to many. Many to many. One to one. And the odd one out... a table that points at itself.

A customer can place lots of orders, but each order belongs to just one customer. Two bars by customers mean exactly one. A crow's foot and a circle by orders mean zero or many. So which table holds the link?

Not customers. Ada's orders, one and twenty-five, would have to share one cell. Nothing can check a list like that, and every new order means editing Ada's row. So the foreign key goes on the many side. Each order stores one customer ID, and Ada's shows up twice. That repetition isn't duplication. It IS the relationship. But what if both sides can have many?

A student takes lots of courses, and a course has lots of students. Ada takes Math and History. Grace takes Math and Art. The links cross, because neither side is the parent. Give students a course ID, and Ada's row has room for one. Math fits... so where does History go? Flip it, and Math has room for one student. Where does Grace go? One foreign key always forces one side to be one.

So give every pairing its own row, in a third table: enrollments. Ada in Math is a row, Ada in History another, each with two foreign keys. So the tangle becomes two plain one-to-manys. That's a junction table. It's not a hack... it gives the relationship a name.

And the pair of keys is the row's identity: student and course, together, make the primary key. Enroll Linus in Math, and that's row forty-nine. Try it again? Postgres says no: that key already exists.
